claims.claim: Usability testing refers to evaluating a product or service by testing it with representative users, who try to complete typical tasks while observers watch, listen, and take notes, in order to identify usability problems.

In a usability-testing session, a researcher (facilitator) asks a participant to perform tasks with the interface while observing the participant's behavior and listening for feedback; the goals include identifying design problems, uncovering opportunities to improve, and learning about the target user's behavior and preferences.

Designers are not users: even the best UX designers cannot get the design right without iterative design driven by observations of real users and their interactions with the design, because there are many variables in an interface and even more in the human brain.

The core elements of most usability tests are the facilitator, the tasks, and the participant; tasks are realistic activities the participant might perform in real life, and the participant should be a realistic user of the product or service being studied.

The classic finding by Jakob Nielsen and Thomas Landauer is that about five participants uncover most usability problems in a qualitative test: a single user typically uncovers roughly 31% of the problems, the first 5-user study finds about 85%, and additional users of the same type mostly repeat known findings.

The five-user rule carries honest caveats: it applies to qualitative testing of a single group of comparable users (distinct user groups each need a few participants, roughly 3-4 per group), it finds most common problems rather than every problem, and precise quantitative measurement such as task times or success rates requires far larger samples.

Qualitative usability testing focuses on insights and observations about how people use a product and is best for discovering problems, while quantitative usability testing collects metrics such as task-success rates and time on task and is best for benchmarks; the two play complementary roles in an iterative design cycle.

The honest framing is to test to learn, not to prove: watch what users actually do rather than trusting what they say they would do or predict they might do, and use each round of testing to find problems, fix them, and test again while changes are still cheap.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Five users versus larger sample sizes
conflictingEvidence.detail: NN/g's own guidance spans both claims: five participants uncover the majority of the most common problems in a typical qualitative study, yet the same source notes that finding all usability problems takes about 15 users and quantitative benchmarks need around 20. The lesson presents these as complementary: five is a qualitative discovery number for one group of comparable users, not a statistical guarantee.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Do not listen to users versus testing with users
conflictingEvidence.detail: NN/g's first rule of usability warns not to trust what users say they would do, which can sound like a rejection of user involvement. The lesson resolves this by noting that usability testing is observational: it watches what people actually do, which is exactly the behavior the first rule points to.

sourceRecords.title: Usability (User) Testing 101
sourceRecords.license: Copyright NN/g; used as reference only
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live via curl on 2026-08-21 (Kate Moran, December 1, 2019, last reviewed July 15, 2026). Supports: usability testing as an observational UX-research methodology in which a facilitator asks a participant to perform tasks while observing behavior and listening for feedback; the goals of identifying design problems, uncovering opportunities, and learning about target users' behavior and preferences; the claim that even the best designers cannot get the design right without iterative design driven by observations of real users; the core elements of facilitator, tasks, and participant; tasks as realistic activities; participants as representative users; the think-aloud method; qualitative testing as best for discovering problems and quantitative testing as collecting metrics such as task success and time on task; and the recommendation of five participants to uncover the majority of the most common problems in a typical qualitative study of a single user group. Facts restated in original prose; no source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users
sourceRecords.license: Copyright NN/g; used as reference only
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live via curl on 2026-08-21 (Jakob Nielsen, March 18, 2000). Supports: the classic finding that the best results come from testing no more than 5 users and running as many small tests as the budget allows; the Landauer-Nielsen model in which a single user typically uncovers about 31% (L) of usability problems and the first 5-user study finds about 85% of problems, with diminishing returns afterward; the recommendation to spend a testing budget on several small rounds rather than one large study; the caveat that the formula holds for one group of comparable users, with 3-4 users per group recommended when testing two distinct groups and 3 per group for three or more groups; and the follow-up guidance that quantitative studies (usability metrics) need around 20 users and finding all problems takes about 15 users. Facts restated in original prose; no source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Quantitative vs. Qualitative Usability Testing
sourceRecords.license: Copyright NN/g; used as reference only
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. Supports: qualitative data are observational findings identifying which design features are easy or hard to use; quantitative data are metrics such as task-completion rates and task times; the two play complementary roles in an iterative design cycle; quantitative results are numbers that need a reference point (a baseline, competitor, or previous design) to interpret meaningfully. No source prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: First Rule of Usability? Don't Listen to Users
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. Supports the honest framing: watch what people actually do, do not believe what people say they do, and do not believe what they predict they might do in the future; users do not reliably know what they want; stated preferences correlate only weakly with measured performance (r = 0.44 for applications, 0.53 for websites in later research). Facts synthesized; no prose reproduced.
